papers.title_in_file: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning for Multiclass Image Classification
papers.version_note: arXiv:2508.18161v1 [quant-ph] 25 Aug 2025; the text is the paper its record names.
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid QCNN preprint that feeds measurements of the qubits discarded at the first pooling layer into a classical dense head and reports accuracy gains on four-class MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and OrganAMNIST splits.

existing.value: The authors state that they evaluate on classical image datasets, and that intrinsically quantum problems such as topological-phase recognition or error syndrome classification remain future work.
quotes: Although our benchmarks focus on classical image data, the hybrid QCNN is independent of how the input state is prepared.
Extending the evaluation to intrinsically quantum problems, such as topological-phase recognition or error syndrome classification, remains a natural direction for future work.
existing.certainty_reason: The Introduction states the evaluation scope and the future-work limit.

existing.note: The sentence is the authors' own, but the comparison behind it is narrower than the stored value reads: two baselines only (Bokhan et al. QCNN and Chalumuri et al. QMCC), four-class splits only, and the 262 parameters are 74 more than Bokhan's architecture, so the model is not the smallest compared.
existing.value: The authors state that, against the QCNN of Bokhan et al. and the QMCC of Chalumuri et al., their model achieves the highest reported accuracies with a compact 262-parameter footprint; the comparison is on four-class splits, and the paper says the recycled-qubit branch adds only 74 trainable weights relative to Bokhan's architecture.
existing.anchor: Sec. VI, results; Sec. VI B, Table IV and text
quotes: our model achieves the highest reported accuracies while keeping a compact 262-parameter footprint.
Table IV benchmarks our 262-parameter hybrid QCNN against two of the most parameter-frugal baselines in the literature
TABLE IV: Comparison of lightweight quantum models on four-class splits.
while adding only 74 trainable weights relative to Bokhan’s architecture.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical comparison from one study.
existing.reader_inference: The text never lists how the 262 parameters are made up: Table I gives 2 x 15 + 2, 2 x 15 + 2 and 2 x 15 quantum parameters per block and the factor k of the discarded head is not given, so the total cannot be recomputed from the text.

existing.note: The three before and after pairs are quoted correctly, and the paper does say all other settings were identical. But the MNIST pair does not come from one split: the text gives 70.0% to 93.3% for MNIST 0-1-2-3 and 60.39% to 88.52% for 3-4-5-6, and Table III lists 68.51% as the amplitude baseline of 3-4-5-6 while 93.55% is the recycled 0-1-2-3 amplitude result in Table IV. The Fashion-MNIST and OrganAMNIST pairs are same-split pairs.
existing.value: The authors report that incorporating the discarded-qubit measurements raised test accuracy from 68.51% to 93.55% on MNIST, from 81.40% to 96.45% on Fashion-MNIST and from 69.13% to 88.50% on OrganAMNIST, against a baseline that omits those measurements while keeping all other settings identical; for the MNIST 0-1-2-3 split the text gives 93.3% against 70.0% for the baseline.
existing.anchor: Sec. VI and Sec. VI A, p.10; Tables II to IV
quotes: test accuracy climbed from 68.51% to 93.55% on MNIST, from 81.40% to 96.45% on Fashion-MNIST, and from 69.13% to 88.50% on OrganAMNIST
a baseline that omits the latter while keeping all other settings identical.
On the MNIST 0-1-2-3 split, amplitude encoding with a (7,1) qubit pair (the probabilities from retained wire 7 & 1) attains 93.3% accuracy versus 70.0% for the baseline
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
existing.reader_inference: Table III puts 68.51 on MNIST 3456 (amplitude) and 70.03 on MNIST 0123 (amplitude); Table IV puts 93.55 on MNIST 0123 and 88.52 on MNIST 3456. So 68.51 to 93.55 pairs two different splits. The text also prints 93.3 where the tables print 93.55.

assertions.value: The authors state that their backbone contains two pooling layers and that no further pooling is applied after the final pair of convolutional layers.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V A and Sec. IV C
quotes: Although our backbone contains two pooling layers, we deliberately recycle only the qubits discarded after the first pooling operation.
No further pooling is applied, leaving the surviving qubits available for measurement and subsequent classical processing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own circuit layout in Sections IV C and V A.
assertions.reader_inference: Section VI A describes the compared circuits as 'six convolutional blocks plus three pooling stages', which does not match two pooling layers in Section V A and Table I.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in the recycled and baseline comparison, the circuit depth is six convolutional blocks plus three pooling stages.
quotes: circuit depth (six convolutional blocks plus three pooling stages)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI A states the circuit depth of the compared models.
assertions.reader_inference: Section V A and Table I show two pooling stages, not three.

assertions.value: The authors state that a general member of SU(4) is specified by 15 independent real parameters, and that each convolutional layer applies copies of a 15-parameter template Uconv to nearest-neighbour qubit pairs.
quotes: a general member of SU(4) is specified by 42 − 1 = 15 independent real parameters [40].
Each convolutional layer in our network therefore applies li copies of a 15-parameter template Uconv(θ) to nearest-neighbour qubit pairs (Fig. 2)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV A defines the convolution template and its parameter count.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints four squared as '42'; the arithmetic is 16 minus 1 = 15.

assertions.value: The authors state that the one-to-one match between parameters and degrees of freedom guarantees that their ansatz is universal for two-qubit gates.
quotes: This one-to-one match between parameters and degrees of freedom guarantees that our ansatz is universal for two-qubit gates
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim argued by parameter counting only.
assertions.reader_inference: A parameter count equal to the dimension of SU(4) is necessary but not sufficient for universality; the paper cites Vatan and Williams (ref. 41) for the decomposition and does not prove it.

assertions.value: The authors define the pooling unit as Upool = CRZ (ϕ1) CRX (ϕ2), in which the control qubit is kept and the target qubit is measured and removed.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV D, Eq. (6); also Sec. IV B, Eq. (4)
quotes: Upool = CRZ (ϕ1) CRX (ϕ2)
in which the control qubit is kept and the target qubit is measured and removed (Fig. 3).
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections IV B and IV D define the pooling gate.
assertions.reader_inference: Section IV B says the target is 'traced out' while Section IV D says it is 'measured and removed'; Section V A says the discarded qubits are measured and their measurements are reused.

assertions.value: The authors state that amplitude embedding is used when the pre-processing output has more than 8 elements and angle embedding otherwise, and that all reported results use n = 8 qubits, allowing up to 256 features.
assertions.anchor: Sec. III A, III B and III 'Choice of encoder'
quotes: Amplitude embedding is selected whenever the pre-processing pipeline outputs a vector with N > 8 elements; otherwise, angle embedding is applied.
In our experiments we set n = 8, allowing up to 28 = 256 features while remaining within NISQ hardware limits [26].
All reported results use n = 8 qubits for a fair comparison with the amplitude-embedding configuration.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the encoder rule and qubit count.
assertions.reader_inference: The pre-processing that reduces an image to 8 or 256 features is not described in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that after min–max normalisation each pixel xi in [0, 1] is converted to rotation angles by the affine map θi = π xi, ϕi = π (2xi − 1).
quotes: After min–max normalisation xi ∈ [0, 1], each pixel is converted to a pair of rotation angles by an affine map
θi = π xi, ϕi = π (2xi − 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III B gives the encoding map.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says each data dimension consumes one qubit yet each feature gets two rotations; with n = 8 qubits this fixes the number of angle-encoded features at 8.

assertions.value: The authors state that two four-component probability vectors are recorded, one from the qubits that remain in the data path after the first pooling layer and one from the qubits removed by pooling, and that each is mapped from [0, 1] to [−2, 2] by the affine rule p → 4p − 2.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV C; Sec. V A 1, Eq. (7)
quotes: We record two four-component probability vectors: one drawn from the qubits that remain in the data path after the first pooling layer
Each vector is linearly mapped from [0, 1] to the symmetric interval [−2, 2] using the affine rule p → 4p − 2
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV C states the readout and rescaling.
assertions.reader_inference: Section V A 1 says the retained qubits are measured after all convolution and pooling stages while Section IV C ties the first vector to qubits remaining after the first pooling layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the centring step greatly improves the conditioning of the subsequent classical layers, and that without it the raw probabilities would enter the classical layers highly skewed, hampering gradient flow.
assertions.anchor: Sec. IV C; Sec. V A 1
quotes: this centring step greatly improves the conditioning of the subsequent classical layers without introducing additional trainable parameters.
would enter the classical layers highly skewed, hampering gradient flow
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no ablation of the rescaling is reported in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text reports no run without the rescaling, so its effect is not separated from the recycled branch.

assertions.value: The authors state that they fix κ = 4 in all experiments, supported by gradient analysis (keeping z in [−2, 2] in the high-slope region of tanh), variance considerations (Var(z) equal to kappa squared over 12, approximately 1.33 at κ = 4) and practical deployment ranges.
quotes: we fix κ = 4 in all experiments.
gradient analysis (keeping z ∈ [−2, 2] in the high-slope, non-saturating region of tanh)
variance considerations (Var(z) = κ2/12 ≈ 1.33 at κ = 4, compatible with Glorot/Xavier)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V A 1 states the fixed setting and its stated justification.
assertions.reader_inference: The variance argument assumes p is approximately uniform; a probability vector over four outcomes sums to one and has mean 0.25, so 4p − 2 has mean −1, not 0. The 'centred at the origin' wording does not hold for these vectors.

assertions.value: The authors state that the retained-qubit head is a single fully connected layer of width m, equal to the number of target classes, followed by a tanh nonlinearity, with m squared weights and m biases, which is 20 trainable parameters at m = 4.
quotes: We pass this vector through a single fully connected layer of width m matching the number of target classes followed by a tanh nonlinearity.
the retained-qubit head contains exactly m2 weights and m biases.
In the four-class experiments reported here (m = 4) this is only 42 +4 = 20 trainable parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V B 1 defines the retained head.

assertions.value: The authors describe the discarded-qubit head as a three-stage dense subnetwork (a class-aligned projection, an expansion of the feature dimension by a factor k, and a contraction back to width m) that injects only mk + m classical neurons, and elsewhere as a lightweight two-layer head.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V B 2; Sec. IV C
quotes: These values are then fed into a three-stage dense subnetwork that mirrors the retained path in width but enhances expressivity:
To uncover higher-order correlations, we expand the feature dimension by factor k:
This design injects only mk + m classical neurons that are lightweight compared to typical CNN heads
those from the removed wires are processed by a lightweight two-layer head that briefly expands and then restores the feature dimension.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V B 2 defines the discarded head.
assertions.reader_inference: The value of k is not given anywhere in the text, so the 262-parameter total cannot be recomputed. Three listed stages and a 'two-layer head' are described differently.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two head outputs are fused by the Hadamard (elementwise) product, merged without adding trainable parameters; one subsection states that the fused vector is treated as the logit output of the network, while another states that it is fed to a final dense unit whose output constitutes the network logits.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V B 3; Sec. IV C; Sec. II; Table I
quotes: Fusion is performed via the Hadamard (elementwise) product:
the two quantum-derived feature streams are merged without adding any further trainable parameters.
The fused vector z is treated as the logit output of the network.
the fused vector is fed to a final dense unit whose output constitutes the network logits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections V B 3 and IV C state the fusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The two statements conflict: Section V B 3 says no auxiliary dense layer is used, while Section IV C, Section II and Table I (FCfinal) describe a final dense layer. Parameter counts differ with the reading.

assertions.value: The authors state that their preliminary trials showed that addition or concatenation offered no performance gain but required more parameters or hyper-parameter tuning, whereas the parameter-free Hadamard product delivered the sharpest decision boundaries.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V B 3, 'Why choose the Hadamard product'
quotes: Our preliminary trials showed that addition or concatenation offered no performance gain but required more parameters or hyper-parameter tuning
whereas the parameter-free Hadamard product delivered the sharpest decision boundaries while keeping the model ultra-lightweight.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim from unreported preliminary trials.
assertions.reader_inference: No numbers for the addition or concatenation trials are reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the discarded qubits are measured immediately after the first pooling layer, when they leave the quantum data path.

assertions.certainty_reason: Section V A 1 states the measurement checkpoint.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum register size, gate depth and noise budget stay unchanged, and that the scheme delivers better performance with zero additional quantum resources and a negligible classical footprint.

assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no resource count is given beyond the parameter totals.
assertions.reader_inference: The recycled model also adds a classical head, and the baseline uses a single fully connected layer, so classical capacity differs between the compared models.
